answers.justification: Haverlow's dispatch probes (C1) and the trailer telemetry, which cannot be edited (C6), both show product at 2.4–3.6°C right up to door-open with no trend, and Haverlow's Q2 scorecard was clean (C14), so the warm readings in E3 do not show product arriving warm.

Median dock-to-chamber time for night-received pallets rose from 44 min to 3 h 52 min, on dock lanes that are unrefrigerated and averaged 15–17°C overnight (C11); the chambers themselves held temperature (E6, C2); and lab profiles show temperature abuse after manufacture (C3).

Chamber air held 1.7–3.9°C, with only two brief defrost alarms, both in week 29 (E6), and the contractor's service visits found no outstanding faults (C2); day-received lots stored in the same chambers saw no rise in write-offs (C11).

Receipt probes are keyed at the receipt-confirmation step around 02:30–03:20 (E3), roughly 3–4 hours after the trailers were emptied by about 23:00 (C6), and the trailer product probe read 2.4–3.5°C at door-open, so the recorded values reflect product after it had sat on the dock.

Corriebank credits rose disproportionately after self-certification began (E7, C13), but the KAM has no hard evidence (E7), genuine spoilage also rose (C3, C4, C11), and no claim-level data has been reviewed.

Night dock-to-chamber time jumped in week 31, exactly when the night team was cut from six to four (E5), while night pallet volume (118→121), the slot schedule and day-shift times stayed essentially unchanged (C11, E5).

The night write-off rate rose from 0.6% to 2.9% equally for Haverlow, Pellridge and own-label lines while the day rate stayed flat (0.5%→0.6%) using the same chambers (C11); the mechanism is a warm dock (C11, C3), and the rival explanation of warm Haverlow arrivals is ruled out by C6.
Haverlow loads arrived at 2.4–3.5°C (C6, C1), and non-Haverlow night lots show the same elevated write-off rate (C11), so Haverlow's arrival temperature does not explain the increase.

Corriebank's credits rose from about £1,250 to £3,100 a week after the 3 August policy change (E7, C13), but genuine spoilage was also rising (C11, C4) and no claim-level data separates the two effects.

It punishes a supplier whose product arrived in specification (C1, C6), cannot meet the contract's 24-hour notice and joint-inspection requirements (C8), would incur capacity fees and 4–6% higher cost (C8, C15), and shifts volume to Pellridge, whose night lots fail at the same rate (C11).
It reverses the change that caused the problem (E5) and directly targets the dock-dwell mechanism (C11), with ongoing monitoring from WMS scan data.
Over-claiming is not established (E7, H5 unknown), and part of the rise in credits plausibly reflects genuine shelf-life loss from dock warming (C4, C11).
The extract is available on request (C13) and would let us test H5 properly, but it addresses the smaller customer-credit part of the rise rather than the DC-stage write-offs (E1).
It switches off a protective receiving control and suppresses temperature information (E3) without addressing the staffing cause of dock dwell (E5, C11).
Temporal order (E5), mechanism (C11, C3) and covariation by shift across all suppliers, with the Haverlow rival ruled out (C6), together justify committing to A2.

ambiguousItems: Q13: A4 could reasonably be 'preferred' as the right complementary step for the customer-credit question, or 'acceptable' because it is evidence-gathering on the smaller part of the problem rather than the lead action.

Q9: R4 could be read as 'causal', since the rise is confined to Corriebank, is disproportionate and starts on the policy date, or as 'association-only', since genuine spoilage is a rival explanation and no claim-level data has been reviewed.
Q7: R2 'causal' versus 'association-only' depends on whether the shift-level comparison counts as ruling out rivals, given there is no intervention yet.
caseProblems: C11's catalogue title ('dock-to-chamber times and DC-stage write-off rates by receiving shift') points strongly at the answer, and the item effectively resolves H2, R1 and R2 on its own.
C6 settles H1, H4 and R3 almost single-handedly; the timestamp gap of about 3.5 hours between trailer door-close in C6 and receipt confirmation in E3 is neat but realistic.

Minor: E7 gives Corriebank's July credits as about £1,250 a week, against total weeks 26–31 customer credits of £2,400 in E1. These are consistent, but the case does not show other customers' credits separately.

rulings.explanation: A2 is the action ranked highest. C6 rules out warm arrivals: telematics are uneditable, show product at 2.4–3.5°C at door-open and show no trend. C11 rules out the chambers: day-received product from the same suppliers in the same CH1–CH3 keeps 0.5–0.6% write-offs. C11 also shows night dock time jumping from 44 min to 3 h 52 min in the week of the crew cut, with flat volume, and night write-offs rising to 2.9% for every supplier. E5 supplies the change and its timing. A2 reverses the change at about £2,300 a week, against a roughly £15,700 a week rise in DC-stage losses, can be undone, and includes monitoring. The open credit question (H5/R4) does not bear on whether to restore night capacity. The blind solver gave no answer, so there is no competing argument for 'insufficient'.

The scale defines 'preferred' as 'among the best next actions', which allows more than one preferred action. A4 is cheap: C13 says a claim-level extract is available on 10 days' notice. It does not compete with A2, and it is clearly the best available step on the one open question. A4 also reconciles claims against delivery lots and receiving shift, which directly separates over-claiming from genuine dock-warming loss. So an analyst could fairly rate it 'preferred' as the complementary step. The key's 'acceptable' depends on the authoring note that only the single leading action is preferred, but neither the case text nor the answer semantics say so. The key's reasoning (smaller component, about £2.7k a week, not the lead) is reasonable, but nothing in the case excludes the other reading.
rulings.fix: Add to the presenting request: "Rate as 'preferred' only the single action that should lead; rate sound secondary or complementary steps as 'acceptable'." This makes 'acceptable' the only defensible answer for A4 and keeps A2 as the sole preferred action.

rulings.explanation: The flag's premise that the rise is 'confined to Corriebank' is false. E1 minus E7 shows non-Corriebank credits also rising, from about £1,150 to £2,000 a week (+74%), which fits genuine dock warming affecting every customer. Corriebank's rise is larger (+148%), but timing alone cannot settle cause. Dock warming began in week 31 and the policy started in week 32, so they overlap almost exactly. Nothing in the evidence shows whether Corriebank's product mix or exposure to night-received lines differs from other customers'. No claim-level data tests whether claims are valid, and C11 excludes credits. The main rival, genuine shelf-life loss, is therefore not ruled out, so 'causal' is not justified and 'association-only' is the careful reading. One correction: the key's rationale says 'no customer comparison' exists. A rough comparison can be derived from E1 and E7; it is suggestive but confounded.
rulings.fix: No change to the evidence is needed. Correct the Q9 rationale to read: "An implicit comparison (E1 minus E7) shows Corriebank's credits rising faster than other customers', but customer mix and exposure to night-received lines are unknown, so the rival is not excluded." Optionally, to close off the 'causal' reading entirely, add to E7: "Corriebank takes most of our Haverlow dairy lines." This makes its larger rise explainable by its greater share of dock-warmed, night-received product.

rulings.explanation: C11 gives a within-site natural experiment. Dock time rose only on the night shift, which had the crew cut and flat volume. Write-offs rose only for night-received lots, from 0.6% to 2.9%, while day-received lots of the same suppliers (Pellridge, own-label) in the same chambers stayed at 0.6%. That controls for supplier, chamber and seasonal rivals; day exposure to the August heat would have hit day receiving harder, and it did not move. Unrefrigerated lanes at 15–17°C for about four hours provide the mechanism. The warm E3 entries and C3's 'temperature abuse after manufacture' fit it, and C6 removes arrival temperature as a rival. The answer semantics explicitly count a natural experiment as grounds for 'causal'; no deliberate intervention is required. Night-only rivals such as handling damage are not supported: the write-offs are condition and shelf-life losses tied to temperature.
